statement: To identify people, animals or objects at a distance, a hunter must use binoculars, never a rifle scope.
In Québec, a hunter must get the owner's permission before hunting on private land, even unfenced, and must ask again at each visit.
If a hunting companion breaks the rules, insist politely but firmly that he comply; hunters must report any poaching.
Air guns propel a projectile by the decompression of a gas, while firearms use the combustion of an explosive charge such as powder.
There are four groups of commercial air guns: refillable air reservoir, pump-lever, piston, and CO2.
Under the federal Firearms Act, air guns with a velocity of at least 152.4 m/s and muzzle energy of 5.7 joules are treated as firearms.
In a spring-piston air gun, compression is done by hand with a cocking lever, which in most cases is the barrel itself.
To load a break-barrel spring air gun: point it safely, tap the barrel down, rest the butt on the hip and fold the barrel fully open, insert the pellet, close the barrel and engage the safety.
Never dry-fire a spring-piston air gun, and never keep the spring compressed more than 30 minutes, to avoid damaging the mechanism.
Because spring-piston guns recoil, rest the forend lightly on the supporting hand for accuracy; a fixed, rigid rest is strongly discouraged.
Air guns use skirted pellets (diabolo); when fired, the skirt expands into the rifling, sealing the bore and giving a spin that stabilizes the pellet.
Hollow-point pellets are designed to flatten on the target rather than pass through it.
Projectile mass is measured in grains; 15.43 grains equal one gram.
The maximum effective range for a quick kill of small game with an air gun is 30 metres (about 100 feet), but its dangerous range is about 640 metres.
A scope is strongly recommended on an air gun, but it must be built to withstand air-gun recoil; a reticle graduated for distance helps account for the trajectory.
Air guns must be lubricated with a non-detergent oil designed for them to avoid damaging the seals; do not oil the inside of the barrel except for storage of several months.
With a break-barrel spring gun, always complete the cocking movement fully, because the barrel can snap back and injure your face or damage the gun.

In an in-line muzzleloader, the primer sits in a cavity at the end of the breech plug; a small hole called the flash hole carries the primer's flame to the powder charge when the hammer strikes the firing pin.
Never use smokeless powder in a muzzleloader designed for black powder or its substitutes: the barrel could burst.
Black powder substitutes are less corrosive, more stable and produce less smoke than black powder; 30- and 50-grain powder pellets are popular because they are easy to use.
Basic muzzleloader accessories: a short starter eases inserting the bullet, a ramrod seats the charge, a bullet puller removes the projectile, and a breech-plug grease prevents the plug from seizing.

To load or unload a muzzleloader, set the butt on the ground secured between your feet and keep your face and hands from ever being over the muzzle; never have a primer in the breech plug while doing so.
Mark the ramrod: a first mark at the muzzle with the barrel empty shows 'unloaded', a second mark with charge and bullet seated shows 'loaded'.
Install the primer only at the hunting site or when ready to fire at the range; without a safety, cock the hammer only at the last moment before firing.
After a misfire or hangfire with a muzzleloader, keep it pointed in a safe direction and wait 60 seconds in case of a delayed discharge before taking any other step.
A hangfire (raté d'allumage) is when the primer fires but the powder does not ignite; causes include a defective primer, damp powder or a blocked nipple.
To unload a muzzleloader, first point it in a safe direction and remove the primer, then remove the powder charge and the projectile.
Muzzleloader safety: never load indoors, never smoke or allow smoking near black powder, never fire if you suspect a double charge, and always remove the ramrod before firing.
After firing at game with a muzzleloader, wait at least 30 minutes, ideally one hour, before starting to search for it.
Black powder and substitutes leave corrosive residue: clean the bore with warm, slightly soapy water, then rinse with very hot water so it dries quickly, then wipe and lubricate.
Store primers and powder separately, ideally locked, in containers used only for ammunition that are not airtight, away from flammable materials and ignition sources.
Good hunting clothing is comfortable, suited to the weather, blends into the surroundings, is silent, does not interfere with shooting and is odourless.
When carrying a backpack, always wear the blaze orange vest over the backpack.
Avoid washing hunting clothes with popular scented detergents; special detergents remove odours and UV reflections, which some game such as white-tailed deer can detect.
Signs of regular game passage include crushed vegetation beds, wallows, browsing (frayed twigs, stripped branches, torn bark), rubs on trees and droppings.
Hunt facing into the wind so game cannot smell you; in Québec prevailing winds come mostly from the west.
A new ground-blind tent should be set up and aired before placing it at the hunting site to remove synthetic odours.
A ground blind is very effective for moose, white-tailed deer, waterfowl and wild turkey, but is not recommended for bear; the tree stand is recommended especially for black bear.
A tree stand gives a better view and a safer shot directed toward the ground, but brings a risk of serious injury or death from a fall and exposes the hunter to weather.
Still hunting means walking slowly and quietly through game habitat, ideally into the wind, with frequent pauses to listen and watch; it needs little equipment and is ideal for beginners.
Still hunting needs little equipment and preparation, making it the ideal technique for beginners.
For small game, still hunting in a group of two or three is most effective; for safety, walk side by side and never lose sight of your companions.
Calling is effective for almost all game but is not used for small game, except the crow and predators such as coyote and red fox.
Rattling consists of clashing cervid antlers to imitate a fight between rivals during the rut, in order to attract a dominant male.
An adult female moose generally has a white, triangular vulvar patch from the base of the tail to the vulva, a long head and a protruding, swollen muzzle.
Seen from the front, a moose calf's head is triangular with a fairly pointed muzzle, while the adult female's head is rather rectangular; the calf rarely travels alone, so beware of a double kill.
For big game, aim at the centre of the heart-lung vital zone, just behind the front legs for cervids and slightly farther back for bear.
Shoot only when the game is still and ideally broadside (perpendicular to the line of fire), with no obstacles in the way.
A cervid hit in the heart or lungs usually jumps and runs off with its head down before collapsing a bit farther; one hit outside the vital zone may wait, stop to look and call out in distress.
If an animal looks abnormal or behaves unusually it may be sick, and it is strongly advised not to harvest it.
After the shot, stay calm, secure your firearm, note the time and your position, and tell your hunting partners to avoid a double kill and get help.
After the shot and once the animal is out of sight, wait at least one hour before starting the search, even if you think you hit the heart or lungs.
At the impact site, move in slowly and quietly without disturbing signs, mark the spot with biodegradable tape or toilet paper, and take a compass bearing of the animal's escape point.
Deeper-than-usual tracks at the impact site generally indicate the animal was hit, as a hit cervid jumps and a hit bear digs its claws into the ground.
Heart blood is bright red and may contain large air bubbles; lung blood is lighter, pinkish and frothy, possibly with bits of lung.
Liver blood is brownish red, dense and forms granular spots; wait ideally four hours before searching.
A hit in the stomach or intestines gives greenish blood in fine droplets, possibly mixed with stomach or fecal matter; bleeding is light, so wait at least four hours.

When the vital zone is hit, there is usually little blood at the impact site but the amount tends to increase along the trail; outside the vital zone, there is more blood at first, then less and less.
A spray of hydrogen peroxide helps spot blood on reddish autumn leaves because it reacts with blood and produces visible bubbles.
When tracking, mark each sign with tape without ever losing sight of the previous ribbon; if the trail is lost, return to the last ribbon and widen the search radius.
If the animal is not found within 200 m of the impact point and there is no more blood, wait at least four hours before resuming or call a blood-tracking dog handler.
When you find a bed (couche) where a wounded animal lay down, place two ribbons and wait at least four hours; each time the animal flees again, wait another four hours.
Never give up the search before exhausting every possibility; mortally wounding and losing an animal then harvesting another wastes the wildlife resource.
Field dress game as soon as possible after the kill to cool the carcass and stop bacteria from multiplying and spoiling the meat.
Wear nitrile gloves when field dressing to avoid diseases transmissible to humans; moisten the animal with water and wear a mask to avoid inhaling airborne hair.
To cool small game and waterfowl faster, avoid piling the carcasses against one another.
A hare acting unusually may have tularemia, shown by white spots on the internal organs; the disease can cause high fever in humans.
A carcass with tularemia must be wrapped in a bag and put in household garbage, then all equipment and hands disinfected.
For game birds, remove the skin, feathers and all internal organs, and do not forget to remove the tail gland (croupion); then keep the meat cool.
To freeze game meat, wrap it in plastic film before putting it in a freezer bag and removing the air; freeze small game within 24 hours unless eaten soon.
Before hunting, tell a trusted person your itinerary, where you plan to hunt, and the day and time you will return, so they can coordinate help if you do not come back.
In remote areas cell coverage is limited and group radios may be out of range, so carry a satellite phone or a distress beacon to alert rescuers.
Carry a map and compass even if you have a GPS, since its battery may die or it may fail; batteries lose much efficiency in great cold, so keep devices close to your body.
When lost in the woods, the main challenges are cold and thirst; do not count on rescuers arriving quickly.

Essential survival items include map and compass, first aid kit, water and purification tablets, high-protein food, two fire sources, multi-tool knife, flashlight, whistle, string, toilet paper, brass wire, and an orange plastic bag and reflective emergency blankets.

If lost, stay calm; first decide whether to stay and wait for help or try to find your way. In daylight, take a bearing toward an identifiable point; if night is coming or you are injured, give first aid and prepare for the night.
Build a shelter considering that prevailing winds come mostly from the west, ideally near water; purify or boil water; eating snow makes you lose much body heat.
Stay dry: if you are soaked, you lose body heat five times faster; insulate yourself from the ground with conifer boughs.
Signal regularly with a whistle, which can be heard more than two kilometres away, and feed the fire with conifer boughs and green leaves to make thick smoke visible for kilometres.
Lyme disease is transmitted by the black-legged tick carrying Borrelia burgdorferi; wear long clothing and a DEET- or icaridin-based repellent, and check your whole body after outings.
To remove a tick, do not crush it and never put oil or liquid soap on it; grasp it as close to the skin as possible with fine tweezers or a tick remover, pull gently, then disinfect.
See a doctor quickly if a growing skin redness, muscle pain, headache or fever appears in the days after a tick bite.
For bleeding, apply a dressing and light pressure and raise the limb; if the dressing soaks through, do not remove it but add another on top and keep pressing.
For a dislocation, never try to put the bone back yourself; immobilize the limb with a splint without cutting off circulation, and leave the boot on if the injury is to the foot.
For a burn, put the area in cold water for a few minutes, then clean it and apply a moist sterile compress; never pop blisters, as the burn could become infected.
In case of internal bleeding, get the injured person to hospital as fast as possible, keep them conscious and give them nothing to eat or drink.
To operate any motorized boat, regardless of length, motor type or power, you must take a boating safety course leading to a competency card (Pleasure Craft Operator Card).
Required on board: oars or paddles, anchor, bailer, sound-signalling device, waterproof flashlight and a buoyant heaving line to rescue someone in the water.
In a boat, never carry your firearm slung over your shoulder, since it could pull you to the bottom if you fall in; tie your gear to the boat to make recovery easier if you capsize.
When wearing chest waders, tighten the belt so water cannot get in if you fall; if they fill, raise your legs quickly so trapped air in the boot feet helps you float.
In a boat, never overload it, never shoot standing up, and always wear a life jacket or PFD that fits your size.
Before each hunting season, consult the regulations to know the rules for the type of hunting you practise.
New hunters are advised to hunt with experienced hunters to improve their techniques, and all hunters should practise regularly to improve shooting accuracy.
